Definition: Unique mobile subscriber penetration rate as a percentage of the total population. Measures the proportion of individuals who subscribe to a mobile service (not SIM cards, which can be multiple per person). Mobile phones are the primary device for internet access in Africa.
revision_notes: Original code of 1 (<25%) directly contradicts its own cited source and comment, which record mobile connections at 175.9% of population (DataReportal/GSMA Intelligence, 2023) -- this is a clear scoring error. DataReportal (GSMA Intelligence data) shows mobile connections consistently at 175-199% of population across 2023-2026, and internet penetration (predominantly accessed via mobile in Libya) at 88-89% of population in 2024-2025. Connections figures overstate unique subscribers due to multi-SIM ownership, so a precise unique-subscriber percentage was not directly located, but the scale of connections penetration and the 88%+ internet-use rate make it very unlikely that unique subscriber penetration is below the 70% top band. Recalculated to 5 (70%+) on this inference; flagged for human review as a top-of-scale promotion given the absence of a directly reported unique-subscriber percentage.
revised_comments: Mobile connections in Libya stand at around 197-199% of the population (GSMA Intelligence data via DataReportal, 2025), reflecting widespread multi-SIM ownership, while internet penetration -- predominantly accessed via mobile -- reached approximately 88.5% of the population in 2025. Taken together, these figures indicate that unique mobile subscriber penetration is very high, almost certainly above 70% of the population.

Definition: Whether the country has enacted comprehensive data protection and privacy legislation. A foundational legal requirement for building trust in digital public infrastructure and for enabling secure cross-border data flows under frameworks like the AU Convention on Cyber Security and Personal Data Protection.
Comments: Law No. 6/2022 on Electronic Transactions provides data protection provisions
revision_notes: The cited DLA Piper source itself states Libya has 'no specific data protection law' but confirms Chapter Seven (Articles 73-79) of Law No. 6/2022 on Electronic Transactions contains dedicated personal data protection provisions, alongside Law No. 5/2022 on Cybercrime. This does not amount to 'no legislation' (code 1) -- it fits 'partial provisions in other laws' (code 2). DLA Piper (last modified January 2024) also confirms there is no dedicated Data Protection Authority (NISSA has an information-security remit but is not a DPA). A further sectoral development -- a Central Bank of Libya personal data protection regulation (Circular No. 18, June 2025) covering banks and fintechs, mandatory from July 2026 -- reinforces a 'partial/sectoral provisions' picture rather than comprehensive legislation. Recalculated from 1 to 2 to match the scale definition; no DPA exists so codes 3-5 are not supported.
revised_comments: Libya has no standalone, comprehensive data protection law, but partial personal data provisions exist within Law No. 6/2022 on Electronic Transactions (Chapter Seven, Articles 73-79) and Law No. 5/2022 on Combating Cybercrime. A national personal data protection law is under committee-level drafting by the National Council for Public Freedoms and Human Rights, and the Central Bank of Libya has issued a sectoral personal data protection regulation for banks and fintechs (Circular No. 18, 2025, mandatory from July 2026). No dedicated national Data Protection Authority has been established; NISSA holds a broader information-security mandate rather than a data protection oversight role.

Definition: Frequency and severity of power outages experienced by businesses and households. Based on World Bank Enterprise Surveys, Afrobarometer, or national utility data. Reflects the quality of electricity supply beyond mere access — critical for running ICT equipment and data infrastructure.
Value Name: Severe (frequent daily outages or regular load shedding)
revision_notes: Confirmed. The 2022 africanews source (18-hour daily outages) still supports code 1, and more recent reporting shows the situation persisting or worsening: African Energy (Oct 2024) reports a gas-output slump deepening GECOL's power crisis with Libya reliant on record diesel imports and no utility-scale renewable capacity as backup; GECOL warned of imminent nationwide blackout risk (LibyaReview, Aug 2025) after plant shutdowns; eastern Libya suffered a complete regional power outage in May 2025; and GECOL has repeatedly announced increased load-shedding hours through 2024-2025. No evidence of improvement was found. Code 1 (Severe) remains the best-supported score.
revised_comments: Libya continues to experience severe and frequent power outages, including extended daily load-shedding and repeated risk of nationwide blackouts. The General Electricity Company of Libya (GECOL) attributes recurring outages to gas feedstock shortages forcing reliance on costly diesel imports, ageing and damaged plant infrastructure, and occasional deliberate disruption of gas supply. Eastern Libya experienced a complete regional outage in May 2025, and GECOL warned of a near-total grid collapse in August 2025 after several generating units went offline. Libya has no utility-scale grid-connected renewable capacity to buffer against these disruptions.
